htheoryR

Native R implementation of the H-theory construction in “Hierarchical entropies” (de Moraes, Brum, Macêdo & Vasconcelos, Physica A 699 (2026) 131899), plus the identifiability theory, estimators, and real-data applications that extend it in an accompanying manuscript (in preparation). The package lives in the htheoryR/ folder of the repository https://github.com/Raydonal/hierarchical-depth, next to the Python package and the pipeline that reproduces the manuscript.

This is a from-scratch R port, not a wrapper: the Meijer-G special-function core (R/meijer.R) is a closed-form reduction derived and verified independently (docs/meijer_derivation.md in the parent repository), backed by Rmpfr for arbitrary precision, and cross-checked against the trusted Python package (../htheory) via a golden-value oracle (data-raw/GOLDEN_PROVENANCE.md).

What it reproduces

  • The original paper’s central claim — maximizing the entropy S[p] under the standard constraints (normalization and mean energy only) returns exactly p_i = B(E_i)/Z — via maximize() and stationarity_residual().
  • The identifiability, estimation, and inference results developed on top of it: the cascade depth N is identifiable from the log-cumulants of a single marginal (log_cumulants_theory(), fit_homogeneous()), with a calibrated parametric-bootstrap test (test_depth()) and measured power (power_curve()).
  • The network application — the same identifiability chain, through Feller’s (1943) mixed-Poisson identifiability, recovers a hierarchical depth from a plain degree sequence alone (fit_homogeneous_network(), test_depth_degrees()).

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("Raydonal/hierarchical-depth", subdir = "htheoryR")

Rmpfr needs GMP and MPFR development headers at compile time (Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt install libgmp-dev libmpfr-dev); nloptr is used for the maximum-entropy optimizer.

A minimal reproduction

The paper’s own worked example (a stretched-exponential cascade, depth N = 1, shape a = 0.5) round-tripped through the whole chain:

library(htheoryR)

energies <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10)
a <- c(0.5); s <- 0.5

# B(E) -> the target distribution p_i = B(E_i)/Z
target <- target_distribution(energies, a, s)

# Maximize S[p] under normalization + mean energy alone, and recover p_target
fit <- maximize(energies, a, s, n_table = 200L)
max(abs(fit$p - fit$p_target))  # small: the round trip closes

Identifiability, applied to a synthetic three-level homogeneous cascade – the depth is recovered from the log-cumulants of the innermost temperature alone, with no access to the intermediate levels (fit_homogeneous targets exactly this homogeneous case, a_i = a; a heterogeneous cascade returns an effective homogeneous depth rather than the literal per-level shapes):

set.seed(1)
T <- sample_TN(c(2, 2, 2), s = 0.5, size = 200000)
k <- empirical_log_cumulants(T, r_max = 3)
fit_homogeneous(k[1], k[2], s = 0.5)  # recovers N_round = 3, a close to 2

# Is a shallower depth (N = 1) rejected by the data?
test_depth(T, N0 = 1, s = 0.5, n_boot = 500)  # p_value = 0: rejected

The network application, applied to a synthetic mixed-Poisson degree sequence – the depth is recovered from the degree sequence alone, without ever observing which vertex belongs to which community:

set.seed(2)
D <- sample_degrees(a = c(3, 3, 3), s = 0.5, lam = 15, size = 200000)
fit_homogeneous_network(D, s = 0.5)          # point estimate
test_depth_degrees(D, N0 = 1, s = 0.5, n_boot = 500)  # rejects a shallow null

Real-data results from the manuscript

The four case studies of the manuscript (email-Eu-core, OpenFlights, wind-tunnel turbulence, and the C. elegans connectome) were run with the Python package’s equivalent functions (scripts/analyze_*.py in the repository, results in results/*.json) rather than this package, since this port’s identifiability/network modules were completed after those analyses. Re-running them with htheoryR, to confirm that the two implementations agree on the reported numbers, is open work.

Performance note

Every Meijer-G evaluation in R/meijer.R costs one or more Rmpfr operations, which are slower per call than mpmath’s compiled series (roughly 0.1-0.5s per call for non-degenerate parameters, more for degenerate ones needing escalated precision). Functions that build a tabulated interpolant over hundreds of points (make_interpolants(), maximize()) can take tens of seconds to minutes as a result — this is a known, accepted characteristic of the current implementation, not a bug; see the comments in R/meijer.R for the numerical reasoning behind the precision-escalation strategy. The test suite marks the slowest checks with Sys.getenv("HTHEORY_RUN_SLOW") == "true", matching the parent Python project’s own pytest -m slow convention — run

Sys.setenv(HTHEORY_RUN_SLOW = "true")
testthat::test_dir("tests/testthat")

before trusting a change to R/meijer.R, R/statfactor.R, or R/maxent.R.

Relationship to the Python package

../htheory (Python, mpmath/numpy/scipy) is the original, trusted reference implementation and remains the oracle this package’s golden-value tests are checked against (data-raw/generate_golden_values.py, data-raw/GOLDEN_PROVENANCE.md). The two are kept independent on purpose — htheoryR does not call into Python at runtime (no reticulate) — so that numerical agreement between them is a genuine cross-implementation check, not a shared-code assumption.
